subtopic: HOUSING-ASSISTANCE FOR HOME OWNERS ADVERSELY AFFECTED BY RISING MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: HOUSING-ASSISTANCE FOR HOME OWNERS ADVERSELY AFFECTED BY RISING MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in connection with a question which I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on April 21 about assistance to home owners, renters and those suffering from high interest rates in Canada.
Let me tell the House that the constitution and amending the constitution will not help one of those home owners, one of those renters. Not one person suffering from high interest rates today when the bank rate is 13 per cent will be helped by all this talk about amending the constitution. Not one hungry person will get a meal from it. Not one person will be employed by it. Not one person will be saved from the high costs of inflation by all of this talk on the other side about the constitution. They are wasting the time of the House and the people of this country when they talk about the constitution, when the economy is a shambles and when they have turned their backs on every promise they made in the last year.
October 6, 1980

Now to come back to housing and interest rates, what kind of promises were made there? In Hansard on November 6, 1979, the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) is recorded as saying:
-it is right and necessary for Liberals to take a new approach and a new look at interest rate policy.
Well, the new look was a pretty quick look. They have done nothing on it. Also on November 6 he said that he wanted-
-action taken now to prevent the hardship this Conservative high interest rate policy is creating for millions of Canadians and their families.
Interest rates today are 13 per cent at the bank, and under this government they went up to 17.5 per cent-17.5 per cent under the policy of that government. When the government is asked when it will produce a policy to help home owners and renters, there is no answer. The Prime Minister does not answer. He gives some easy patter about the great Liberal principles of helping those who most need the help. Those who need the help now are the people who have had to take out mortgages and renew them at the present rates of 14 per cent or 15 per cent. The Liberal rates of interest are down slightly now from what they were a few months ago under the early leadership of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), 17.5 per cent. We want to know when gentlemen opposite will bring in a great policy to help home owners and to help renters. It was the present Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) who all last fall opposed our mortgage interest and property tax deduction program which would have helped middle and lower-income Canadians who had homes or wanted to acquire them. He and gentlemen opposite fought that policy so that it never went through. They said they would bring in a tremendous shelter allowance program. I have the quotation here from the gentleman who was the housing critic at that time. He is now the Minister of Employment and Immigration. He is hiding in that portfolio. Here is what he said as resported in Hansard at page 1017 of last fall:
-if there is a requirement to raise interest rates, there is an equal requirement to help those people who are hurt by those interest rate increases.
What action is he and his government taking to help those people who are hurt by interest rate increases which now appear to be necessary because the government is now in power? What has happened to the government opposite that voted for a non-confidence motion and defeated our budget because it did not lower interest rates, it did not cut taxes and it did not stimulate the growth of the Canadian economy? Where are the honourable geniuses opposite, those chameleons, those people who think they are born to rule? When will they lower the interest rates? When will they cut the taxes? When will they stimulate the growth of the Canadian economy? We have a Minister of Finance who is the most silent minister of finance ever in our history-and he is the Minister of Finance who has the most to be silent about. He has a shameful record of seven months of complete inactivity in comparison to the finance critic who is now the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray). That gentleman was tremendously active in the fall of 1979 when he had such fantastic policies. He was so confident that he went on CTV on
Adjournment Debate
February 7, 1980. He was asked the question: "Would you lower interest rates?" He replied: "Yes 1 would". Question: "Would you be prepared to resign your seat if the government didn't carry through on that policy?" Herb Gray: "Yes, 1 would.' That was February 7, 1980. What happened afterwards, Mr. Speaker? Interest rates went up. They were then 15 per cent, the prime bank rate. They went up to 15.75 per cent on March 13, then up to 17.5 per cent. And did the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce have the decency to resign? He did not. He went to Japan to tell the Japanese what he was going to do about the car imports from Japan. They wouldn't even let the Dash-7 Aircraft land at the airport in Tokyo. He was going to straighten out the auto pact. He went down to Washington and that is the last we have heard of the auto pact from the great honourable Herbie. Not another word on the auto pact. This was from the man who was going to force the interest rates down and save the home owner. He was like a vacuum cleaner gone berserk when he was finance critic. But we have heard nothing from him, Mr. Speaker. Not another word have we heard from him. And now the bank interest rate is up to 13 per cent again.
By the way, here is the housing critic, the promise to home owners, Mr. Axworthy:
The government could have started where the real problem lies and could have provided something for rental assistance.
That was November, 19, 1979 in the House of Commons. There was going to be help for all occupants. The great Liberal Party that is all heart was going to help not only home-owners, they were going to help the renters. Everybody in the country was going to get help from hon. gentlemen opposite-a shelter allowance. Now, they have been in power seven to eight months, Mr. Speaker. And they have not helped one home owner, they have not helped one tenant, they have not helped one renter, they have not helped one person who occupies a rathole. They do nothing to help anyone and they have now got a majority so we cannot get any answers from them.
It is useless to ask the Minister of Finance a question. He is what I call the Celtic oracle. He is the most silent oracle since the Delphic oracle. And now we hear he is to bring in a budget between October 15 and October 31. God help us.

Well, this is what the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said in a recent speech to the chamber of commerce. Last year he had the solutions to everything. This year he warned the business executives they would be "unwise to expect too much too soon by way of economic recovery". Herbie out of power is going to solve the problems of the world in no time. Herbie in power says it would be unwise, gentle-

October 6, 1980
Adjournment Debate
men, to expect too much too soon. Do not rush the government. We have a majority after all. He says "circumstances permit no magical fiscal solutions to the cyclical economic downturn" such as a stimulative budget. No longer can we expect any solutions from his government. Uncle Herbie is in power. Now what he says is that circumstances permit no magical fiscal solutions to the cyclical economic downturn. Cyclical? It's sickacle, s-i-c-k-a-c-l-e, that's what it is, this picture of hypocrisy, rank, stinking hypocrisy, Mr. Speaker. I do not like to use strong language but in this case 1 cannot avoid it. He went on to say this:
Double-digit inflation threatens to plague Canadians for some time to come-
Well, isn't that nice news to give the chamber of commerce? He is not too worried about it.
He says that double-digit inflation threatens to plague us for some time to come. He says, "Don't worry about it, we Liberals are in power, don't worry about double-digit inflation, after all it is worth it to have us back. You can have a sense of confidence now that we are here looking after your energy problems. We are going to crush Alberta and British Columbia. We are going to gut confederation. We are going to end this federation. We are going to impose our own solutions about the constitution."
He says, "Don't worry about inflation, don't worry about high interest rates, don't worry about the fact you are unemployed, don't worry about the fact that you are starving half to death, because after all we are fixing the BNA Act. We are going to repatriate that from Westminster. We are going to bring it over and put it up in the Peace Tower, and everybody can feel that much happier because Canada will work that much better by the time we get this back. We think that we can keep this fuss going for another year. We are going to extend our honeymoon. We usually only have a honeymoon for five or six months but we are going to extend it for a year and a half because everybody in Canada is so thrilled with this move we are making to repatriate the unrepatriatable-the constitution, the BNA Act or whatever it is."
He says, "on the way we are going to ask the British parliament to do the job we can't do here. Us old colonialists are going to ask Aunt Maggie Thatcher". She is the only hope for the government opposite, and she is a Tory. The government opposite must go on its knees to Aunt Maggie Thatcher and ask her to amend the Canadian constitution without the consent of the provinces."
I am a bit off my topic, Mr. Speaker, so I had better sit down and end by saying that it is a most unsatisfactory situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: HOUSING-ASSISTANCE FOR HOME OWNERS ADVERSELY AFFECTED BY RISING MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was under the impression after reading the orders of the day that the hon. member who just sat down would be dealing with a question about housing. As he indicated, he has strayed somewhat. However, I have prepared a response to
that question which was asked of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in my absence earlier.
1 would like to respond and preface my remarks by saying that 1 will give some examples of how this government has acted to help the people who most needed help in the situation to which the hon. member opposite has referred, that of rising interest rates. I would like first of all to draw his attention to my announcement on March 26 which directed government action toward those people involved in the AHOP program.
The hon. member will be interested to know that between March 26 and July 31, 1980, 2,168 AHOP accounts were reviewed. Of these only 55 required extension assistance under that program, notwithstanding the dire plight which the hon. member has painted. This support was made available to reduce borrowers' payment of principal, interest and taxes to 30 per cent of their income where possible. The benchmark of 30 per cent of income should be directed toward meeting those shelter costs. This benchmark is used widely in the industry and it refers to the amount which people as a rule should be paying toward those costs in an average budget.
AHOP borrowers who renewed their mortgages before that announcement, which is the question that was initially asked of the Prime Minister, were also considered as candidates for assistance. 1 say that because those AHOP mortgages renewed before March 26 were direct CMHC mortgages. They were not indirect mortgages which the corporation secured under the insurance program of private borrowers.
For the people in this category a program was made available to reduce the interest rate to 8 per cent. The gross debt service in all cases was reduced to 30 per cent. For this reason there was no necessity to make the program retroactive- interestingly enough, this was the question that was asked of the Prime Minister initially.
The hon. member has expressed concern about support for lower-income Canadians. He said that nothing, but nothing, had been done to assist those Canadians. Mr. Speaker, this government shares his concern for those Canadians.
That is why 1 was pleased to announce in June an increase of 5,000 social housing units which are allocated across the country. Some of them are in St. John's, Newfoundland which benefited by this allocation. 1 would say the facts are there to support the government's action.
In terms of what is happening in the industry, I am pleased to indicate that the starts in September show that the seasonally adjusted annual rate has rebounded to 166,500. This activity introduces some sign of recovery in the industry. With that recovery the pressure for accommodation and the pressures that spill over to other areas should be somewhat moderated. I am hopeful that it is a trend for the future.
October 6, 1980

subtopic: ENERGY-DEVELOPMENT OF TAR SANDS AND HEAVY OIL RESOURCES
ENERGY-DEVELOPMENT OF TAR SANDS AND HEAVY OIL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 24 1 posed a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). I asked if he had taken into consideration the cost to the Canadian economy of a minimum of a one-year delay in the Alsands project in northeastern Alberta. He replied that he was not causing the delay and had not taken it into consideration. He indicated that this was Alberta's delay. Because Alberta had given the approval, he said, it was up to Alberta to take action.
I take exception to this, Mr. Speaker, because 1 think it is a total misrepresentation of what actually happened during the negotiations.
Mr. Menzel, chairman of the Alsands project, announced the cancellation of a $50 million Winter Works program for this year. He also indicated that they were prepared to cancel the 1981 budget allocated for next year and that by January 1, 1981, they would be ready to shelve the program if the sunset clause comes into effect, and partners in the Alsands consortium withdraw. If any of them pull out, the project will be cancelled. He gives the reason as the lack of an oil pricing agreement.
That does not mean that one province is holding it up, Mr. Speaker. It means that this government cannot make an agreement with Alberta. First, the government said that the price would be set unilaterally at $32 per barrel. The Alsands consortium, the Shell Oil group, said to the government, "Give us the world price. Tax us at the top. We cannot gamble $8 billion and put it in a hole in the ground, not knowing that we will get a return."
What kind of return are they asking for? The same, Mr. Speaker, as you would get if you invested in an apartment building anywhere in Canada or if you invested in a high office tower. That is the kind of return they are asking for.
The mechanism is in place for the federal government to impose a tax on excess profits and it has always been there. But the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources went to Alberta last week, in a big show and offered $38 per barrel. The companies asked for world price, saying, "We are sinking $8 billion into the ground in northeastern Alberta to help with our energy supply."
A delay of one year would add $1 billion to the cost of the project, which is presently set at $7 billion. Officials of Imperial Oil told a House of Commons standing committee last week that the government's failure to reach a settlement on an oil pricing agreement meant they were ready to pull the plug on their project. That means $14 billion, which is ready and waiting to be invested in the future of our country.
As a result of the delay, inflation alone will add $1 billion to $1.2 billion to the cost of both plants. When one plant goes on stream in 1985-86 it will produce 130,000 barrels of oil per day and the other one will produce 140,000 barrels. The cost of 200,000 barrels of imported crude per day for a year, at today's price of $38 per barrel-assuming that is still the price
Adjournment Debate
in 1985-86-would be $2.8 billion. This is money going right out of the country to Venezuela, Mexico, Iraq and Iran. Canada's reserves from conventional crude are declining. This whole mess is moving beyond an economic situation. It is clearly a matter of our survival. It is not going to matter much what the price of oil offshore will be if we cannot buy it because it is not available. We have seen what can happen in the Middle East. We know what can happen with an unstable supply that can be cut off, and in a matter of six months we could go begging for oil.
Until the Alsands plant receives the green light, orders from Ontario for iron and steel will be sitting waiting to be placed, orders for metal fabrication will be sitting waiting to be placed and transportation equipment will be sitting waiting to be placed strictly on the go-ahead of this one plant, Alsands. This means an injection into the Ontario economy of $6.2 billion over the life of the project. That is a five-year injection, and that is one plant alone. For two plants one can double the figures.
There must be a fog prevailing on the government side of the House. It goes beyond normal bounds of reason that ministers opposite cannot sit down and work out an agreement to get those two megaprojects off the ground, particularly when our supply of energy is so crucial. In 1985 and in 1986 oil will be imported. Alberta and the producing provinces will not be able to meet the demand of Ontario, let alone of Quebec and the maritimes.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-DEVELOPMENT OF TAR SANDS AND HEAVY OIL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government's commitment to the Alsands oil sands project and Imperial Oil's heavy oil project is clearly evidenced by the recent proposal of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) for an incentive for oil sands production of $38 a barrel for 1981. This incentive price would be escalated annually by the consumer price index, with the provision that it not exceed the international oil price. This will provide the industry with both an attractive return and a new certainty in the further development of non-conventional oil projects. Our impression is that this approach will be welcomed by the industry. In fact, what we have offered appears to be what one of the potential participants seeks. This proposal is moreover in keeping with the government's promise to provide a new Canadian blended price which incorporates the cost of non-conventional and enhanced recovery methods of production.
The Alberta government, on the other hand, has not accepted this proposal and hence has caused the delay in the approval of these important projects. The federal proposals which were placed before the Alberta government were based upon the commitments which we, in this government, have given to the Canadian people. We are determined to achieve a resolution of oil pricing and revenue sharing in a manner consistent with those commitments and with our energy principles.

October 6, 1980
Adjournment Debate
The government's promise to provide a fair price for Canada's energy was implicit in our announced intention to invoke the force majeure clause which revoked the agreement that international prices would automatically apply for oil sands and heavy oil development. When the original agreement was signed, international prices for oil were under $13 a barrel, not $38 a barrel, which is nearly a threefold increase. Much of this increase occurred over the last year due to the vagaries of the international marketplace. Canadians should not have to pay OPEC-related prices for Canadian oil.
I see that the hon. member who asked the question has left the chamber. It is evident that 1 have deflated him and refuted his argument. 1 will conclude by saying that the fundamental issue of oil pricing is whether prices will be set at levels which are fair and reflect supply conditions in Canada. Although oil sands projects will no longer be tied to international prices,
they will be able to proceed with confidence on the basis of a price regime much more favourable than that applying to the traditional oil fields of western Canada. This intention is in full recognition of the fact that oil sands production is more costly than production from southern Alberta oil fields and therefore requires a more favourable price schedule.
The proposal which the federal government has made to Alberta represents what is a reasonable resolution of the issues which divide us. It is a generous but balanced package, which guarantees large and growing returns to the producing provinces, but is also consistent with federal energy policy. It is Alberta which has delayed and keeps the Alsands and the heavy oil projects from proceeding.
